Mission Accomplished: Smashing The Memory Wall

For decades, software engineers have spent immense effort executing complex bit-twiddling techniques to manually simulate spatial locality within their codebases. However, by treating the cache hierarchy as a data structure worthy of native optimization, we have moved this entire paradigm directly into the processor’s hardwired logic.

Driven by the Z-Order address layout, intelligent barriers powered by distributed Counting Bloom filters, the Tropf-Hertzog range engine, and macro-level 4 KB block management, system memory is effectively transformed into a perfectly organized, multidimensional map. We have eliminated protocol overhead, unburdened the interconnect fabric, and demonstrated that it is possible to permanently break through the memory wall – finally providing compute cores with a cache hierarchy that natively understands the geometry of data.

Cristian Vasile is a long-time reader and intelligent commenter at The Next Platform, and I highly value his comments over the years. (Yes, I am aware that the new CMS we have has destroyed our comments. I am working with the team to try to fix this.) Vasile spent a decade on various software and technical lead positions at Citibank Romania and is now a senior technical business analyst at Integrated Data Systems SRL, a consulting organization based on Bucharest. He had some innovative ideas on how to eliminate the memory wall, and I am pleased to have presented them to you. If you have a burr under your saddle about something and you have the technical chops, I am always happy to let you have the soapbox for a story. Reach out.

item.title: Operationalize AI At Scale With HPE And Nvidia
item.description:
SPONSORED POST: While many organizations have AI projects underway at various stages of maturity , most are experiencing challenges scaling AI across their IT landscape. That is because many AI strategists have yet to work out how to build, operate, and extract value from their AI infrastructure.

Without a formal, top-level plan for AI, key capabilities and requirements get lost, and the full value of AI is never realized.

What is needed is a pre-integrated, full-stack environment that simplifies the deployment, scaling and governance of enterprise AI.

This is where the "AI factory" concept is gaining ground. An AI factory is a specialized computing environment designed to manage the entire AI lifecycle, from data ingestion and training through to fine-tuning and high-volume AI inference. Its primary "product" is intelligence, measured in token throughput, which in turn drives innovation, decision-making, IT automation and future AI applications.

HPE AI Factory with Nvidia is a pre-integrated infrastructure solution with HPE services provided from development to deployment to ongoing support for AI initiatives. It combines Nvidia's accelerated computing and software with HPE's secure infrastructure, software, control plane, and services, to scale as the organization’s needs grow.

The question that follows is how the AI factory model maps onto the main challenges enterprises face when they try to run AI at-scale.

In this Hot Seat interview, James Hayes puts that question to Thierry Pienaar, HPE fellow and Chief Technology Officer for HPC & AI worldwide at HPE, and Kaushik Shirhatti, VP, AI factory at Nvidia. He asks them how the AI factory model is reshaping enterprises thinking about AI and how it is accelerating customer projects.

Pienaar and Shirhatti explain that AI no longer sits in a deployment vacuum, and that today's enterprise-wide rollouts carry risks older architectures were never built to absorb. Secure operations that scale across segments become a core requirement, particularly as deployments take in a widening range of personas, workgroups and, increasingly, agentic inputs.

Security that load-balances intelligently, so that demand does not overwhelm the system, matters just as much. Sovereign AI is another priority: the balance between innovation and control now shapes how customers meet their growing sovereign AI mandates, which have become central to AI governance.

You will learn:

• How AI factories can enable workload-specific architectures.

• How agentic AI is being used within the AI factory context.

• How HPE AI Factory with Nvidia meets the range of challenges customers face, and how it stands apart in its market segment.

• New joint innovations the HPE and Nvidia partnership is bringing to customers.

Learn more about how sovereign AI beats compliance challenges and feeds local innovation with HPE and Nvidia here.

item.title: Despite Hefty Capital Investments, The Cloud Starts Paying Off For Oracle
item.description:
In its latest quarter, Oracle set record revenue levels and, importantly for the first time in its five decade history, its first quarter of one fiscal year was larger than the fourth quarter of the prior fiscal year. This is bucking the normal cycle where salespeople try to cram as many deals into Q4 to get a big bonus, which understandably makes Q1 naturally a weak one.

Granted, it was only eight-tenths of a percent growth sequentially, so it was not huge. But it is a different pattern, and suggests that Oracle, which had a revenue backlog of $664 billion as the quarter ended, is going to see its cloud infrastructure business go superlinear if not exponential. And that is being driven by backlog converting into sales.

“We would expect acceleration to continue in the remainder of fiscal 2027 as we convert more RPO into revenues,” Hillary Maxson, Oracle’s chief financial officer, explain on a call with Wall Street analysts going over the numbers for Q1 F2027. “We now expect around half of our RPO to convert into sales over the next 36 months.” If you do the average on that, it works out to $27.7 billion per quarter. It will be smaller in fiscal 2027 and larger in fiscal 2029, of course. Exactly how much is hard to predict from the outside of Oracle, of course. And then the other half of the backlog will still be there out beyond fiscal 2029.

In the quarter, Oracle posted revenues of $19.18 billion, up 29.6 percent and up a smidgen sequentially (but not down). Operating income rose nearly twice as fast, up 57.3 percent to $6.73 billion, and net income grew even faster, up 62.6 percent to $4.76 billion.

Under any normal circumstances, with Oracle approaching a net income to revenue ratio that predates its heavy cloud investments, such numbers would make Wall Street gaga. But they are worried about a future where Oracle plans to spend $90 billion to $95 billion in capital expenses for fiscal 2027. Oracle just raised $19.9 billion floating stock, and thanks to $11.4 billion prepayments largely from cloud customers, it had a cash flow of $23 billion in the quarter. But it also blew $28 billion on capex, which makes its cash flow a negative $5 billion.

Here is the monster table breaking down revenues and operating income for Q1 F2027 for Oracle and going back to Q1 F2026:

The Oracle Cloud division made $11.61 billion in sales, up 61.5 percent and up 17.1 percent sequentially. Software license sales took their typical Q1 dive, down 65.2 percent sequentially and down 14.5 percent year on year as customers continue to shift to cloud-based subscriptions from perpetual licenses plus support contracts. The software support business, which is basically an annuity that Oracle cashes in on every quarter, had $4.9 billion in sales, down 1.2 percent.

Hardware sales – yes, customers still buy Oracle infrastructure rather than renting it – was up 15.5 percent to $774 million, but was down 16.2 percent sequentially. In the year ago period, hardware sales were actually up 6.3 sequentially to $670 million. Operating income for hardware is under pressure as component prices for systems are going haywire thanks to the GenAI boom, where demand is outstripping supply on nearly all semiconductor fronts, and have hit a low of 63.7 percent of revenue compared to an average north of 73 percent in the two years before the component price hikes hit. Interestingly, the operating margins are under the same pressure in the Cloud And Software group, no doubt caused by component prices for the iron Oracle buys for its cloud as well as increasing expenses for all components of a datacenter buildout.

Services, which includes implementation of Oracle’s myriad applications in its Fusion and NetSuite portfolios as well as many legacy application stacks that don’t change much and for which Oracle can rightfully charge an arm and a leg to support because customers have not moved ahead, rose by 4.8 percent to $1.41 billion.

The exciting bit for the Oracle top brass is that Oracle’s cloud infrastructure (IaaS) revenues rose by a factor of 2X to $7.4 billion in the quarter and was up 27.6 percent sequentially. By comparison, Oracle’s SaaS software revenues only rose by 9.2 percent to $4.2 billion.

Here is the drilldown Oracle presented to Wall Street on its IaaS and SaaS revenues in the Cloud division:

Oracle’s cloud database business – which one could argue should be considered SaaS because it is software, but then again it is systems software running on Exadata hardware that has been highly tuned for it – was up 26 percent to $900 million. Within this segment, the multi-cloud implementation of the Oracle database sold as an infrastructure service rose by 4.5X year on year. It is very likely a small part of the overall database slice of IaaS sales.

Sales of CPU and GPU capacity comprise around 88 percent of Oracle’s cloud IaaS sales and generated $6.5 billion in sales, up 2.5X year on year. This is the conversion of AI backlog to running workloads. Oracle added 850 megawatts of its own infrastructure capacity with more than 300,000 GPUs and untold CPUs to rent out by the hour during fiscal Q1, which is 3X the capacity Oracle delivered in Q4 F2026 (around 280 megawatts). Oracle added 1.16 gigawatts of capacity last year, with 400 megawatts coming in Q3 F2026, leaving 480 megawatts of capacity being installed in 1H F2026.

For comparison, the OpenAI Stargate buildout, where Oracle is installing the infrastructure for the AI model builder, in Abilene and Shackleford in Texas (3.2 gigawatts) and Dona Ana, New Mexico (2.2 gigawatts) and Port Washington, Wisconsin (1.3 gigawatts) and Saline, Michigan (1.4 gigawatts) are supposed to added up to 8.1 gigawatts. Oracle says it has secured 10 gigawatts of power for three years through fiscal 2029. Those are datacenter power numbers, so the infrastructure power draw is probably on the order of 70 percent of that, or about 5.7 gigawatts. If that is comprised of Nvidia systems, that would cost $227 billion to deliver just the infrastructure at the expected $40 billion per gigawatt cost that Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang has talked about. If it is a mix of homegrown OpenAI Jalapeno accelerators (for inference) and Nvidia GPUs (for training), it probably blends to around $30 billion per gigawatt, then it will cost $170 billion for the hardware.

Clay Magouyrk, co-chief executive officer at Oracle and the person in charge of the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure business, told Wall Street that 131,000 GPUs (almost certainly “Blackwell” B200s and B300s from Nvidia) went into the Abilene datacenter for OpenAI in the quarter, and 69,000 went in during Q4 F2026. At this point, OpenAI has taken delivery of 618 megawatts, or 75 percent of the total capacity, of the infrastructure going into Abilene from Oracle. The new GPT-6 Astra model was trained on this iron in Abilene. The Shackleford datacenter is being fleshed out with “Vera-Rubin” systems from Nvidia, and OpenAI will get its hands on this initial capacity sometime during Q2 F2027.

For the moment, the GPU economics are working in the favor of Oracle as GPU and XPU demand far outstripped supply. (How much is unclear.) The majority of the GPUs in Oracle’s fleet – which has to number 1 million or more GPUs by now – are four years old or older, and yet they are commanding higher and higher prices because compute need is bigger than compute capacity. It is not hard to see these devices being in use for three, four, or even more years into the future – and they probably pay for themselves in three years. Across all of the GPUs that came up for renewal in Q1, the portfolio of renewals priced out at 20 percent higher than their original contracts. GPU utilization was at 97.9 percent in Q1, which is IBM mainframe-class utilization.

I will end with some interesting notes on Oracle’s own use of AI.

Mike Sicilia, co-chief executive office and the person who runs the software side of the Oracle house, said on the call that Oracle would be announcing a new agentic AI accelerator at its AI World event next month that would use GenAI to deploy Oracle’s applications in the field at a much faster pace than can be done with human implementers today – and at a much lower cost. Implementation costs for ERP suites can be significant

“Working alongside Oracle and customer teams, AI agents will automate and orchestrate implementation at an unprecedented scale, compressing SaaS deployments from years to months and months to weeks,” said Sicilia. “It is really the power of these things together that reinforce my belief that the growth of our applications business is only going up from here.”

Customers running their Oracle applications in the OCI infrastructure tapped embedded AI capabilities in their applications 150 million times in Q1, which is a 42 percent sequential growth, and AI agents were launched more than 3.5 million times, which was nearly double sequentially from Q4 F2026. Customers, says Sicilia, have over 2,300 agents in production on their Oracle applications. In the high-end Fusion ERP suites alone, customers burned 900 billion tokens.

Oracle doesn’t care about the SaaSpocolypse. It cares about using AI against its SaaS apps, making them more useful even if they are no more sticky.

“AI changes this dynamic,” Sicilia explained. “Rather than asking every employee to navigate and execute a process exactly as a system expects, AI agents can perform tasks using the organization's established workflows and business rules. Employees then shift to overseeing agents, resolving exceptions, and applying human judgment where it matters most.”

item.title: Broadcom Rides Rocketing Trend For Custom AI Accelerators
item.description:
Back in March, when looking out into the future of the custom XPU and networking ASIC chips as well as the other chippery that Broadcom sells that goes into AI clusters, I posited that Broadcom, more than AMD or Intel, might become the biggest counterbalance to Nvidia in the GenAI boom . And that it would be getting a little competition from and help from Marvell in this task.

This is turning out to be even more prophetic than I thought, based on the revenue forecast that Hock Tan, chief executive officer and legendary conglomerate builder at Broadcom, provided to Wall Street when going over the third quarter of fiscal 2026 financial results. We will cut to the chase scene here and just show you a table of Broadcom’s AI-related chip sales since F2022 including the blunt – and ebullient –forecast Tan provided:

Broadcom was already helping Google get its homegrown TPUs designed and through the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co foundry and packaging for seven years when the GenAI boom hit. And basically, between F2022, when the GenAI boom started, and the F2028 forecast, that custom AI XPU business plus AI networking and that other chippery going into AI systems will grow by two orders of magnitude from $2.6 billion to $230 billion. The US military budget for the fiscal year just ended was $1 trillion by comparison. Then again, the worldwide consumption of pizza – the world’s most multinational food – was $230 billion in 2024, which I just learned through reading Ten Tomatoes That Changed The World by William Alexander.

Broadcom has secured the HBM memory, chip wafers, and packaging to fulfill this revenue stream for AI compute and networking capacity, and Tan said if the demand is higher, it can add more capacity.

Tan warned Wall Street to not expect quarterly updates to that forecast, but wanted to make it clear that some big money was going to rolling in during the coming years and basically to tell Wall Street to take a chill pill on the GenAI bubble bursting.

Across the six XPU customers that Broadcom has – Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta Platforms for sure, and possibly ByteDance (which owns TikTok) or Apple for the other two, but Amazon Web Services is using Broadcom for packaging and integration for Trainium 4 – there is about 30 gigawatts of total compute capacity, which suggests that you can install XPU systems for somewhere around $12 billion per gigawatt – not including the CPUs, memory, and racks. You are probably around $15 billion per gigawatt when you add those components in. This compares favorably to the $18 billion per gigawatt for Nvidia “Grace-Hopper” systems (which do include CPUs and memory as well as all of the GPUs and interconnects needed to make a rackscale machine) and $40 billion per gigawatt for Nvidia “Vera-Rubin” systems.

Tan said on the call with Wall Street that it would ship “multi-tens of billions of dollars of TPUs annually over the next several years” to Google. “We have consistently delivered the fastest time to market for TPUs from product definition to production without the need for resubmits. We believe these are very deep moats for any competitor to cross.” So forget all of the talk about Marvell, MediaTek, or Alchip stealing the TPU business. It is all about who gets the HBM allocations anyway. . . .

Anthropic is deploying 1 gigawatt of “Ironwood” TPU 7 accelerators this year, will be deploying 5 gigawatts of TPU 8i systems in 2027, and in 2028 Anthropic wants 10 gigawatts of the follow-on TPU 9. Tan said that Anthropic was on track to be its largest XPU customer in 2027 and would sustain that in 2028. (Presumably these are numbers for Broadcom’s fiscal years, not calendar years, but Tan did not say fiscal when referring to these numbers.) That means Anthropic is buying more TPU iron by the grace of Google than Google itself is. As one of the AI model builders with tons of cash flow and a strong balance sheet, you would think Google would be buying more TPUs than anyone else. But Google is a cloud, and cloud customers want Nvidia GPUs.

Crazy, right?

OpenAI has chosen Broadcom to do its chip shepherding for its “Jalapeno” XPU, and is on track to buy 1.3 gigawatts of stuff from Broadcom for its Jalapeno clusters in 2027. In 2028, Broadcom thinks OpenAI will deploy another 5 gigawatts of Jalapeno ASICs and its follow-on, which will make OpenAI its second biggest XPU customer, knocking Google down to number three on the list.

Crazy, right?

The follow-on OpenAI chip, which we do not know the code-name of, is approaching tapeout, according to Tan, and the two companies are working on the third generation XPU design now.

With Meta Platforms, Broadcom will deliver three generations of MTIA devices between now and the end of fiscal 2027, and across those three generations of MTIA accelerators – which we drilled down into back in April – from now and the end of fiscal 2028, Broadcom has a line of site on 3 gigawatts of capacity.

The AI boom inside of Broadcom is not just AI XPUs, and in fact is dominated by networking. The 100 Gb/sec and 200 Gb/sec SerDes variants of the Tomahawk 6 Ethernet switch ASIC are selling like hot cakes, and all of the hyperscalers and clouds that are using Broadcom to shepherd their homegrown XPUs are using Tomahawk 6 for scale out networking on their AI clusters. The Tomahawk Ultra variant of the 6 series chips, which drives down latency in the Ethernet stack so it can be used for scale up coherent memory interconnects for XPUs inside of rackscale machines, is having surprising adoption and is being deployed now at some customers with the ramp progressing through fiscal 2027 as new XPUs are coming to market.

And by the way, the 204.8 Tb/sec Tomahawk 7 Ethernet switch ASIC, which has not been announced yet but which uses 400 Gb/sec SerDes and which gives you 3.2 Tb/sec per port with eight lanes per port, has just taped out and will presumably be seen in switches starting in early calendar 2028 and maybe in late calendar 2027.

One last thing and then I will dig into the Q3 F2026 numbers with you. I fully expect for Broadcom to start shepherding CPUs, and very likely focusing on packaging with a little design work as it is doing with Fujitsu for its forthcoming “Monaka” Arm Server CPU . Fujitsu as well as the six XPU customers are using Broadcom’s 3.5D Extreme Dimension System in Package (XDSiP) chiplet stacking, which puts stacked DRAM as well as stacked CPU chiplets into a package. With the CPU total addressable market growing from $26 billion in 2025 to $220 billion by 2030 and with every hyperscaler and cloud builder making its own Arm server CPUs, I think Broadcom will branch into CPU shepherding. I do not think Broadcom has any interest in designing its own Arm server chip and trying to sell it to these tech titans. This is why it sold off the “Vulcan” processor to Cavium Networks all those years ago.

I do think it is possible that Broadcom will help customers integrate CPU tiles onto their XPU tiles if they decide to hardwire their CPU to XPU ratios. But I also think that having a big memory address space on the CPU (albeit a slower one) is beneficial to XPUs that have to skimp on HBM or other stacked memories because of the scarcity of capacity for those memories. So an external CPU might be the safest bet.

We shall see.

In the third quarter ended in early August, Broadcom raked in $29.59 billion in overall sales, up 85.5 percent year on year and up 33.4 percent sequentially. Operating income was $15.96 billion, up by 2.71X compared to Q3 F2025. Net income grew even faster, rising by 3.17X to $13.09 billion, representing a very nice 44.2 percent of revenues.

Say what you will, but Tan knows how to squeeze a lot of money out of the companies he buys and runs. It is so much better to be a chip shepherd indulging the egos of the tech titans then to try to sell a finished XPU or CPU to them. None of them want to use whatever any of their rivals are using, except X86 CPUs and Nvidia and sometimes AMD GPUs, and they only tolerate that because they are clouds and their customers demand it and because of the shortage of CPU and GPU capacity.

Broadcom ended the quarter with $23.98 billion in cash, but it still has $59.42 billion in debt thanks to the VMware acquisition.

In the quarter, Broadcom’s Semiconductor Solutions group had $20.84 billion in sales, up 127.4 percent, with an operating income of $12.71 billion, up 143.3 percent.

The Infrastructure Software group, which includes VMware and a bunch of other legacy enterprise systems software, had sales of $8.75 billion in Q3, up 29 percent, and operating income was an IBM mainframe-class 84 percent of revenue at $7.35 billion, up 40.7 percent. My model says that $5.52 billion of that was for VMware licenses and support, with the remaining $3.23 billion for other legacy software. But take those numbers with a quarter of a shaker of salt, given that I am extrapolating into the void because Broadcom doesn’t give out much in the way of details about its software business.

Above is my guesstimate on how the old Broadcom divisions are doing. Use another quarter of the salt shaker on that chart, again because Broadcom doesn’t really talk much about these businesses anymore. I probably will stop after this quarter, too.

And finally, that brings us to Ai versus non-AI sales in the chip business. Here is a pretty picture on that:

And there is at table outlining the AI versus non-AI breakdown:

AI-related revenues added up to $16.74 billion, up 3.22X from a year ago and up 54 percent sequentially. Of that, $12.22 billion was for AI compute and $4.52 billion was for AI networking.

item.title: Startup d-Matrix Will Pair Its Raptor Memory-Based XPU To Nvidia Rackscale Iron
item.description:
Engineers with startup d-Matrix have spent the past seven years putting together the pieces of what would become a platform of hardware and software designed to speed up AI inferencing workloads while driving down the costs. The company has been focused on inferencing since its founding in 2019, “when not many people even knew what inference was,” co-founder and chief executive officer Sid Seth said.

Since that time, the demand for faster inferencing has skyrocketed, with the rise over the past year of agentic AI tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and the introduction of OpenClaw helping to push inferencing workloads past what GPUs like those from Nvidia and AMD can handle on their own.

“Over the last twelve months, there has been an explosion of low-latency inference across many different applications,” Seth told journalist and analysts during a briefing this week. “Now, with the arrival of cybersecurity applications, low latency tokens are in huge demand. Because of this explosion in low latency inferencing, the demand for inference has really shot off the charts.”

After seven years of development, d-Matrix, armed with more than $500 million in funding – including from Microsoft's M12 venture arm – in June introduced its first inference accelerator platform, Corsair, which takes a memory-centric approach that executives claim can help run inferencing workloads ten times faster than Nvidia GPUs alone.

Now, Corsair is being paired with Nvidia’s “Blackwell” GPU accelerators in a rack.

The XPU tightly couples the memory , such as SRAM or 3D-RAM, with GPUs and CPUs in the same rack to accelerate the generation of tokens and reduce the associated costs. In a disaggregated environment, GPUs are best for the compute-intensive prefill phases of the inferencing workload, where context tokens are processed, while Corsair, like Nvidia’s Groq 3 LPX accelerator, is better at the decode portion, where the AI model is generating code or other kinds of responses to      queries from people or other models.

Building off of its acquisition in April of the datacenter business of GigaIO, d-Matrix also rolled out its SquadRack reference design, which was built with Arista Networks, Broadcom, and Supermicro.

“Our entire approach is predicated on doing more with the capital people deploy in our compute,” Seth said. “We are able to run really, really fast compute. We do more inference with a little amount of time, and we have made a very energy-efficient solution with the memory-centric computing. That allows us to do more with less of these resources – money, time, and energy. We can hopefully, over time, alleviate the need to build out more datacenters.”

With Corsair on the market for a matter of months, d-Matrix is now talking about its follow-on, the Raptor platform, which d-Matrix detailed during the recent Hot Chips 2026 show , and has put the Lightning platform – which will feature a multi-high DRAM stack – on the roadmap. Raptor, which will tape out by the end of the year and be released in the fourth quarter of 2027, includes a 3D-RAM accelerator that features a 4 nanometer compute die manufactured by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co fused atop a custom DRAM die at a 36-micron pitch that will deliver 100 TB/sec of bandwidth.

With Raptor, D-Matrix uses a variant of the chip-on-wafer package that’s used now for HBM packaging. It will combine a DRAM memory chip and a SRAM compute chip.

A new partnership with Nvidia will help d-Matrix extend its reach deeper into enterprise and HPC datacenters as well as AI labs, hyperscalers, the big cloud builders, and the neocloud upstarts. The partnership, announced Thursday, will make d-Matrix’s Raptor XPU platform available through Nvidia’s MGX reference architecture, deployed as part of Nvidia’s AI factory offering. Seth said Raptor needs a “house to put it in,” and that while building its own liquid-cooled rack was an option, Nvidia offers an existing ecosystem.

“This is truly the fastest way we feel of getting this amazing path-breaking technology that we are building at D-Matrix into the market with quick scale, with a robust supply chain to back it up and with a partner who is deployed in every datacenter across the world,” he said.

The partnership will also include future versions of d-Matrix’s XPUs, including Lightning.

Nvidia’s AI factory business is expanding rapidly. In announcing the company Q2 2027 numbers, chief financial officer and executive vice president Colette Kress said the revenue opportunity for the AI factory platform has grown from about $18 billion per gigawatt since the “Grace-Hopper” rackscale systems in 2022 to $40 billion per gigawatt now with the forthcoming “Vera-Rubin systems . That’s the opportunity d-Matrix is signing up for.

Key to d-Matrix’s plans is NVLink and NVSwitch, Nvidia’s high-speed interconnect for coherently linking GPUs, CPUs, and other accelerators to its rack-scale MGX architecture, which includes the Vera CPUs, the Rubin GPUs, Bluefield-4 DPUs, Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs.

d-Matrix will use the same NVLink compute tray, seen on the left below, but rather than Vera-Rubin chips, it will house Raptor XPUs as well as Nvidia’s Vera CPUs and Bluefield DPUs, and will use ConnectX and Spectrum-X networking for scale out. It will plug into the liquid-cooled NVL144 MGX rack, on the right, and d-Matrix will use the NVLink switch tray. The rack itself will hold 144 Raptor XPUs.

The rack also will feature 2.3 TB of 3D-stack DRAM fast memory at running at 100 TB/sec inside each card with an aggregate memory bandwidth of 7.2 Petabytes per second in a single rack. There also is the option of using the Raptor rack as a companion to Nvidia racks running Vera-Rubin GPUs.

“The beauty of this solution is we take the Raptor trays, plug them into the same NVL144 MGX rack architecture, which is widely deployed across many datacenters, and we get instant access to those datacenters,” Seth said.

At Hot Chips, d-Matrix showed the results (below) of two AI models – Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 and Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 – running on a rack of Raptor chips. With GLM 5.2, d-Matrix got about 3,000 tokens per second per user of performance, with the Kimi model reaching 1,000 tokens per second per user. Seth noted that the vendor can scale this across eight racks.

Jesse Clayton, principal product marketing manager for Nvidia’s Data Center GPU business, said the d-Matrix partnership illustrates Nvidia’s architectural approach, offering a platform that he called “completely fungible” and “vertically integrated, but horizontally open.” Vendors essentially can use as much of Nvidia’s technology stack – which also includes Groq 3 LPX accelerator rack – as they want, while plugging in their own offerings. NVLink Fusion ports open the platform to other silicon.

We will be doing a deeper dive into the Corsair and Raptor architectures shortly. Stay tuned.

item.title: HPE Sees No Customer Pushback On Rising Datacenter Equipment Costs
item.description:
The GenAI wave is indeed lifting almost all of the boats. While Dell has become the largest original equipment manufacturer in the world – a title that the original Hewlett Packard used to have after it bought Compaq in 2001, which had previously eaten Tandem and Digital Equipment Corp to embiggen itself – Hewlett Packard Enterprise is still in the top five and is still the server maker of choice for millions of companies worldwide.

This matters more in the long run than capturing a few AI system deals worth billions of dollars. And besides, HPE could not get the GPU allocations from either Nvidia or AMD to grow its business any faster than it is doing. The big will get bigger faster, as Dell shows.

And as the company’s financial results for its third quarter of fiscal 2026 show, HPE is finally seeing its fortunes improve and is set to help drive AI on various compute and networking engines into enterprises, sovereigns, service providers, and maybe some of the smaller neoclouds.

In the quarter ended in July, HPE posted revenues of $12.21 billion, up 33.7 percent year on year and up 14.4 percent sequentially. Thanks to cost controls and a richer mix of machines as well as passing through price increases on CPUs, GPUs, DRAM, flash, and networking, operating income was up by a factor of 5.6X to $1.39 billion, and net income rose by 5.5X in sympathy to $1.51 billion, representing a very healthy (for a box shifter, mind you) 12.4 percent of revenues. This is one of the best quarters in the company’s history in the datacenter, and you have to go back to the Unix systems boom of the late 1980s and early 1990s to find profitability in systems that is in the same league as what HPE has just turned in.

HPE ended the quarter with $6.22 billion in cash and investments, up 11.6 percent compared to the year ago period.

Here is the monster table describing HPE’s new groups and divisions, which were announced a few quarters ago:

The Cloud & AI group is by far the company’s largest business, lumping together servers, storage, financial services, and tech support for all that gear. The Networking group, which has the acquired Juniper Networks as its core but which also includes various HPE Ethernet switches, including the Slingshot HPC-centric version of Ethernet that its Cray supercomputing unit created two generations of machines back, is smaller but is growing faster.

In Q3, Cloud & AI sales rose by 25.4 percent to just a tad over $9 billion, and was importantly up 17.3 percent sequentially, showing that HPE is converting its backlog of AI systems and more traditional systems to revenue even as its backlog is growing. Cloud & AI operating income was up by more than 3X to $1.54 billion, which is wildly more profitable than the HPE systems business has been in a long, long time. Within this group, server sales were up 35.3 percent to $6.77 billion, while storage rose by 10.2 percent to $1.29 billion. Financial services was steady freddy at $883 million. HPE does not provide operating income at the division level.

The Networking group had sales of $2.89 billion in Q3, up 74.9 percent as HPE is getting an increasing attach rate for networking to its servers and storage. (This was the whole idea of buying Juniper.) However, campus and branch switching is still the main driver of this business, with $1.44 billion in sales, up 31 percent year on year and comprising just under half of revenues. Routing, which is a big business with service providers who don’t want to always buy Cisco Systems gear, drove $788 million in revenue, up by a staggering 3.7X year on year. Despite all that you hear, hyperscalers, cloud builders, and neoclouds buy a lot of routing equipment to lash their datacenters together.

One such company is none other than Oracle, which has its own cloud and which has a deal with HPE to supply it with routers and switches after Q3 F2026 closed. The bulk of this deal is for Juniper QFX switches based on the 102.4 Tb/sec Tomahawk 6 switch ASIC from Broadcom , which launched in June last year and which is shipping now. The deal also includes using Juniper’s AIOps software to manage the networks. HPE says this deal is part of a potential multi-gigawatt datacenter rollout and might span multiple years. As part of the deal, HPE gave Oracle warrants for up to 4.2 million HPE shares, and ahead of announcement day these would have been worth north of $200 million. The actual vesting for these warrants was not disclosed.

Like other deals we have covered, the idea is to use vendor shares as a way to cover some of the cost of the hardware acquired, and the deal itself makes the shares more valuable as soon as it is disclosed, which helps the vendor and the customer alike.

This Oracle deal is not to be confused with a $3.5 billion deal that HPE has inked separatelywith an unknown hyperscaler. “It is a very important use case,” Antonio Neri, HPE’s chief executive officer, explained on the call with Wall Street analysts going over the numbers.  “It is a hyperscaler customer, but think about them as an enterprise customer who is going to use our AI inferencing for their own internal usage. So our strategy has not changed from selling large amount of infrastructure for them to serve, like it used to be in the past the cloud business. This is about a multi-billion-dollar AI inferencing for their own internal usage as an enterprise customer. It just happened to be they are labeled as a hyperscaler customer.”

Back to drilling down into the HPE numbers for the quarter, then.

HPE booked just under $1.6 billion in AI server revenues in Q3 F2026, up about 7 percent from the year ago period. HPE added $2.4 billion in new AI system orders in the third quarter, and we presume that HPC systems are being put in this bucket because there is not an HPC deal that is not also an AI deal at this point. HPE’s AI server backlog stood at $6.8 billion as the quarter came to a close. For AI networking, which it has begun to track separately since acquiring Juniper, orders were $700 million for AI-specific systems and the backlog stood at $800 million. HPE did not disclose the AI-related revenues for the Networking group. But we can tell you that AI networking orders are up by 3.5X year on year.

The traditional, non-AI server business was booming in Q3, with sales up 52 percent to $5.17 billion. As was the case with Dell, there is a natural upgrade cycle for vintage HPE ProLiant servers in the installed base, and the machines that companies are buying to replace this old gear are packed with CPUs, DRAM, flash, and hard drives. Such fat boxes have inherently higher costs (justified by the density of the machines and the power savings they deliver compared to racks of older machines) coupled to ever-increasing costs for just about every component in the system.

HPE’s history in the datacenter business is, of course, much longer than the GenAI boom and even the tenure of its current top brass. We have been tracking the company for four decades, and the dataset we have built tracks the core datacenter systems business of HP and then HPE since the Great Recession, which was definitely a dividing line in history. Take a gander at how the financials of this core systems business has changed in the past two decades:

The GenAI boom started helping lift revenues in fiscal 2024, and the addition of Juniper to the HPE portfolio has only accelerated that. And HPE has set record datacenter revenues for core systems – servers, storage, networking, tech support, and financing for the gear – for the past five quarters in a row. Yes, it is dwarfed by Dell, Supermicro, Inspur (IEIT), and Lenovo in the server business, but when you add in networking and financing, the gap is not as large.

Going forward, revenue growth depends on GPU allocations that HPE and its customers can get, and that depends on the power and facilities that those customers can line up.

In any event. HPE’s core system revenue in the third quarter came in at $10.49 billion, up 35.1 percent and up 15.6 percent sequentially. Our allocation of operating income shows the core systems business generated $1.86 billion at the middle line.

Looking ahead, HPE expects to do $13.9 billion to $14.8 billion in business in its fiscal fourth quarter, with the Networking group expected to grow by 11 percent to 13 percent and the Cloud & AI group growing by 60 percent to 72 percent. Clearly, it depends on how the power and facilities line up to GPU allocations.

As far as Neri is concerned, demand is there and people are rebalancing their budgets and increasing them in a way that we have not seen since the Dot Com boom. And there is not a lot of pushback on costs.

“At the beginning of this hyper cycle, on the cost, obviously they were a little bit in shock, and they're trying to navigate through that timing by focusing on understanding the trends and looking at the spot market and the like,” Neri explained. “Once they understood that and understood that particularly on AI, you need to go faster, they figured it out. Look, waiting is not an option. But they're getting smarter about where to land their budgets and how to optimize for these token economics. When you do it on premise, and we do that ourself, and we share the number, we can see up to 60 percent cost benefits on a token basis.  And so, no, I don't see hesitation at this point in time, and that's why demand continue to be exceptionally strong.”

item.title: Dell Says AI Will Drive 75 Percent Of Datacenter Demand By 2030
item.description:
It may have taken many years and what we presume was a certain amount of patience as Michael Dell watched his custom server maker rivals working for the hyperscalers and clouds get the vast majority of GPU allocations, but AI is a driving force for the company that bears his name.

And so is an inevitable server upgrade cycle that has been a long time coming – and that has been delayed in part by AI spending and then accelerated as companies try to free up power and space in their datacenters by modernizing their application and database server fleets to make way for power-hungry AI servers.

This is the opposite of the perfect storm, which is compounding bad news. As far as I know, we don’t have a name for that converse, so I guess we can just call it a harmonic resurgence. And now that the partners of Nvidia and AMD can make more GPU accelerators than they could several years ago, Dell is getting a lot more GPU allocations, and I think a disproportionately larger part of AI system orders because it has its supply chain and factories in order and can actually line up iron to run against its swelling GenAI revenue backlog.

In a conference call going over the company’s second quarter of fiscal 2027 financial results, Jeff Clarke, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman, said that it took eight quarters to get 3,200 customers who had bought an “AI factory.” And the next 3,300 customers were closed in only three quarters, for a total of 6,500 unique organizations that have deployed AI systems with PowerEdge brands on them. A lot of those customers are Tier 2 clouds and service providers as well as neoclouds and sovereigns, but now large enterprises are also looking to Dell, their traditional server supplier, to not only upgrade their aging iron, but to supply AI clusters for inference and maybe some training as well.

Dell’s server business is hitting on all cylinders, and Clarke explained that there were over 1.2 million servers in the Dell installed base that were at the PowerEdge 14G generation or older. The 14G machines were announced in 2017 and ramped in 2018. So this iron in on the order of eight years old or older. That is a long time to keep a server in the field, and the current 17G machines from two years ago and the forthcoming 18G machines due next month allow workloads to be consolidated massively. Clarke pegs it at anywhere from six to eight of these vintage servers collapsed to one 17G system, and anywhere from twelve to fourteen for one 18G machine.

These are much more heavily configured 17G or 18G machines that customers are buying to do consolidations, and so they are inherently more expensive. Dell is also passing on increasing costs for DRAM, flash, CPUs, and other peripherals, which further boosts revenues for traditional servers.

In the quarter that ended on July 31, Dell booked $41.11 billion in product sales, up 71.8 percent year on year and up 7.9 percent sequentially. Services revenues pottered along and were flat at $5.86 billion.

Combined product and services revenues totaled $46.97 billion, up 57.7 percent, and thanks to Dell maximizing its CPU, GPU, DRAM, and flash allocations, further optimizing its massive system manufacturing operations, and boosting margins on PCs, operating income for the company rose by 3.1X to $5.36 billion. Net income in the quarter was $4.13 billion, up 3.55X year on year and representing 8.8 percent of revenues. This is the highest level of profitability for Dell in our coverage since the Great Recession a decade and a half ago excepting Q2 F2020 and Q3 F2022, when it was selling off parts of the company and profited nicely from that.

Still, as you can see, it takes a lot more dollars to drive an incremental gain in net income. Dell has moved from the kind of margins one of the large grocery store chains or its original design manufacturer (ODM) rivals “enjoy” of around 2 percent to 3 percent to something akin to a software company in a very aggressive and non-legacy part of the market of around 8 percent to 10 percent. That is an improvement, but Dell is working hard to get there. And we have not looked at the numbers yet, but we strongly believe that Dell is doing much better than its original equipment manufacturer (OEM) peers like Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, Supermicro, and the rebadged Inspur now known as IEIT Systems, which rules in China.

It is interesting to note that Dell’s debt load is on the rise again, even if it is nowhere near where it was when Dell acquired EMC and VMware a decade ago and took itself private a few years later. The debt load went below $30 billion after VMware was spun out and was trending responsibly down over several years as the cash got pinched. Both cash and debt are rising at roughly the same rates, which is good, so the relative net debt is not changing much despite the heavy investment that is required for AI systems.

Michael Dell is the fifth richest man on Earth, and unless Wall Street is making a fuss, there is no reason not to do stock buybacks to drive up the net worth of Dell, the man, and his wife, who together own 41 percent of the shares in the company. Similarly, they get 41 percent of dividend payments, too. All of this cash – $2.2 billion in the second fiscal quarter – could be used to pay down debt, as could some of its $14.25 billion in cash and investments.

But as I said, Wall Street doesn’t seem to care. Particularly with Dell’s revenues growing faster than its debts.

Let’s drill down into Dell’s server racket a bit.

Dell’s server and networking business, which is mostly servers, rose by 2.1X to $26.93 billion, up 9.1 percent sequentially. The company’s storage business, which is built on the EMC foundation, was up 25.8 percent to $4.85 billion.

Clark gave an update of sorts on the Project Lightning parallel file system aimed at high end AI workloads, something that has been cooking for the past two years and that is aimed at taking on Lustre (controlled by DataDirect Networks) as well as storage from VAST Data, WEKA, and Everpure (formerly Pure Storage). Lightning is not based on Isilon’s OneFS, a very good HPC file system that has a long history outside of Dell and that is at the heart of the PowerScale high-end systems that are managing very large files. Lightning, by contrast, is aimed at workloads that have tons of small I/Os against block storage running in flash.

“Lightning, our parallel file system designed for native AI use cases, we continue to have the product out in the field,” Clarke explained. “We continue to see interest. It is still a relatively new product. It is in beta at several customers. We are in runoffs against other competitors with the product. That will continue. And as it builds momentum, I am certain we will give you an update in the future. But that's where Lightning is at the moment.”

The competition is probably not worried at this point.

Add all that revenue up and the Infrastructure Solutions Group had $31.78 billion in sales, up 89.2 percent year on year, with operating income of $4.78 billion, up 3.25X. The $15 billion PC business (up 20.2 percent year on year) at Dell only had $1.14 billion in operating income (up 42.2 percent).

Dell has been explicitly breaking its AI systems business separate from its traditional server and networking business for the past two quarters, and I have been doing the math back to Q4 F2022 with my own model to show just how fast this AI business has taken off for Dell.

Dell’s AI system business was bigger than its traditional server business a year ago, and it is very likely that the gap will continue to be large. But traditional servers are, as I said at the top of this story, booming and the gap closed quite a bit for at least this quarter and it looks like it will surpass AI server sales in Q4, if you can believe it.

To be precise, Dell sold $16.4 billion in AI systems, double from a year ago and almost the same as in Q1 F2027. Traditional servers plus networking hit an all-time quarterly high that makes the Dot Com boom look like a joke, with sales of $10.53 billion, up 2.2X from the year ago period.

On the AI systems front, Dell ended the quarter with $95 billion in bookings, and $60.9 billion of that came within the quarter. That backlog is 8.1X larger than a year ago.

Looking ahead, Dell expects around $19 billion in AI system sales in Q3 and another $22.5 billion in Q4, which would bring the full year to $74 billion. If you do the math on the ISG forecasts and back out traditional servers, you get $15.6 billion in Q3 and $25.1 billion. Yup, traditional servers are set to eclipse AI servers in Q4, just as “Vera-Rubin” systems from Nvidia are ramping to full volume.

We live in crazy times.

“As we see it, agentic demand is reshaping the datacenter in underlying infrastructure,” Clarke said. “Inference is past training, and it is pure demand in our industry. We think the tokens that inference drives is going to grow 87X to 3,600 quadrillion tokens by 2030. Training demand grows 5X to 850 zettaflops by 2030. Enterprise agentic is expected to be the single largest workload by 2028. We are expecting AI to be 75 percent of all datacenter demand by 2030, adding 200 GW of power over that same time frame, and half of that, we believe, is right in our sweet spot with our customers, the neocloud, sovereigns and enterprises. And if you look at that math, we think the opportunity in front of us is more than $1 trillion over that time frame. And we believe we are well positioned. We believe that our model is differentiated, that our engineering is differentiating ourselves with every customer that we interact with. The scale of our deployment capabilities is unmatched globally.”

Well, Supermicro and IEIT Systems would probably argue with that. And so would Sanmina, which took over the ZT Systems business from AMD. So would Quanta Computer and Foxconn as well. The point is, Dell is right in there, competing with the ODMs and dwarfing its OEM peers. That is what is truly unexpected. And it all comes down to Nvidia allocating GPUs to Dell to get them into neoclouds, sovereigns, and large enterprises so Big Green can lessen its dependence on the hyperscalers and cloud builders that are all making their own XPU accelerators as well as buying tons of GPUs from Nvidia.

item.title: Nvidia Expands Its Open Source AI Presence With $12.9 Billion Hugging Face Buy
item.description:
Nvidia co-founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang was among hundreds of executives with other tech companies who in July signed an open letter about why open source AI and, particularly open weight AI models, are important to US leadership in the overall AI space, from accelerating innovation and expanding access to cybersecurity and sovereignty.

In a post on X about the letter, Huang wrote that “AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. ... The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.”

It was part of Huang’s years-long vocal support for open source AI , which Nvidia has backed with such advancements as its growing Nemotron family of models , specialized open platforms and frameworks that include Cosmos for physical AI, Isaac GR00T for robotics, and Clara for biomedical research. There also open tools for developers, including the recently rolled out NeMo SwitchYard , an open routing library for AI agents.

Nvidia’s embrace of open source AI makes sense. As Huang likes to remind the industry, his company is the world’s largest AI computing platform and its GPUs fuel much of today’s AI workloads, making it the richest enterprise, with a market cap north of $5.4 trillion. The global open AI market is expanding rapidly and, in turn, is expanding access to AI, which drives even more demand for Nvidia’s GPUs and AI infrastructure .

Now Nvidia is spending $12.9 billion of its vast wealth to become an even bigger player in the open AI space, following through on its reported intent to buy Hugging Face, which over the past ten years has grown to become the central platform, repository, and community for open source AI – referred to at times as the “GitHub for machine learning” – that hosts millions of AI models, includes a massive collection of open datasets for model training and evaluation, and offers open libraries.

The deal is expected to close sometime in the first half of 2027, pending regulatory approval.

Bending The Curve To Make An Inflection Point

Hugging Face chief executive officer Clément Delangue said that he and the other founders believed the company had reached an inflection point, that the open source AI community had grown to the point that continuing to support as it scaled required more resources than Hugging Face had. In an interview with CNBC , he pointed to Anthropic’s upcoming IPO, which some reports indicate could raise as much as $130 billion .

As we have pointed out before, there are very few companies that can afford to frontier train AI models and give them away, but as the very existence of Hugging Face clearly demonstrates, there are plenty of developers who can train smaller models for domain specific tasks and set them free. Nvidia may be the only company that can open up frontier models, given the huge revenue and margins it has on AI hardware at the moment. (See Nvidia Is The Only AI Model Maker That Can Afford To Give It Away . )

Delangue said that in AI, there are “two tasks,” with one being proprietary APIs that large numbers of organization are outsourcing their AI jobs to. The second is “where open source AI is available to everyone and everyone can actually become an owner, a builder of AI, and not just renting it or using it from other people. It became clear that there were these two paths and that we needed to double down on open source AI to really distribute the technology as much as we and all over the world.”

According to the companies, Hugging Face has more than 18 million developers and more than 200,000 enterprises using the platform, 3 million models, 1 million applications, and 500,000 datasets. And open source AI is a dynamic and fast-growing environment. Huang said Nvidia is the largest contributor to Hugging Face.

In August, Hugging Face released a report looking at statistics between January and July, with numbers showing a surge in open models released by Chinese labs (below) like Alibaba with Qwen (which the report said had become the “community’s base model”), Moonshot AI with Kimi, and DeepSeek.

Meanwhile, US companies AMD and Nvidia published the most new models. (below)

I

Another interesting trend: AI agents have become the number one user on Hugging Face Hub (below), which the company said could significantly change the numbers in the next report.

In an interview with journalists, Delangue said he first approached Huang this summer with the idea of Nvidia buying Hugging Face. Huang told CNBC his first reaction when approached by Delangue was that Hugging Face should stay independent, but he heard that other companies were interested in buying it.

“At a time when open models are accelerating, this is really a very, very delicate time,” he said. “I want to make sure that it has all the support necessary. Open models matter greatly to our company, which is the reason why we invest so much ourselves. There are so many industries beyond languages that benefit from open models, and we're completely committed to it. It's really important to us that it lands in a good place, and Nvidia is a great home for them.”

He noted that another indicator of the growing space that open models are taking up, noting that cloud services providers that use Nvidia technologies represent about half of the vendor’s business. The other half is driven mostly by open models.

“Nvidia is growing in both directions and our fundamental goal is just to make sure that AI advances as quickly as possible,” he said. “It's really, really important right now as the open models are really accelerating, that we make sure that we provide Hugging Face the platform to continue to scale and for the resource for them to scale and extend the open model ecosystem and community.”

Security A Driver Behind Hugging Face’s Decision

That rapid expansion of open source AI models was the key driver behind the decision by Hugging Face executives to approach Huang. However, Delangue pointed to a security incident over the summer that also fueled their thoughts. In July, hundreds of OpenAI agents that were being evaluated escaped their testing environment that was isolated from the internet and breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure . For the industry, the actions of the agents – which also included collaborating via a message board they created without authorization – was a warning shot about the threat that autonomous AI represents without sufficient guardrails.

It also was a lesson for Hugging Face, whose initial response was hindered cause the commercial, proprietary AI models it was using for security triage includes guardrails that blocked the analysis of the exploit code. The company got around the blockage by moving its forensic analyst to Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 open-weight model that was running locally on its infrastructure.

“When that happened, what we realized is that we needed open models,” he said. “If you remember, we couldn't defend ourselves with a proprietary, closed source API, so we had to use open models to defend ourselves. It did show the importance of open source.”

item.title: Optics Still Driving Marvell’s AI Business More Than Custom Chips
item.description:
The datacenter has become the dominate factor in driving the business of chip maker and chip shepherd Marvell, and the growth in this business is almost exclusively coming from components for AI clusters. While it is exciting that Marvell has big deals with Amazon Web Services, Google, and others for custom chips, this business is still relatively small. Optical components for networks as well as switching are still driving the bulk of the sales.

Legacy chips in the aimed at telcos and other carriers, enterprise networking, and consumer and industrial devices – which once were a bigger part of a much smaller Marvell – are still humming along with their ups and downs, but Marvell does not really talk about these much anymore except as they are lumped into a single group. Like this:

Nvidia, for what it is worth, has done the same thing, lumping everything that is not part of its datacenter business into a group called Edge Computing. In fact, this chart looks very much like Nvidia’s chart, although the numbers on the Y axis are a hell of a lot smaller and the exponential curve is not quite so steep for Marvell. At least not yet. But watch as AI networking and custom XPUs and CPUs take off among the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders. Marvell is becoming every bit as much of a counter balance to Nvidia’s largesse in GenAI as is Broadcom.

In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on August 1, Marvell had $2.17 billion in datacenter product sales, up 45.7 percent year on year and up 18.5 percent sequentially. My model says that legacy enterprise networking, which should arguably be added to the datacenter, brought in an additional $266 million in the quarter, and I think it rose 37.4 percent year on year. Admittedly, any breakdown in the old legacy divisions Marvell used to talk about are guesswork, since the company has not talked explicitly about their revenues since Q3 F2026.

Add all of those legacy businesses up, and they rose by 10.1 percent in the quarter to $567.8 million. The datacenter part of the Marvell business is now 79.3 percent of total sales, and if you add in enterprise networking, that drives it up to 89 percent of revenues.

Just for fun, here is how the datacenter business compares to the other former divisions in my model:

Unless Marvell talks about these explicitly at its financial analyst day coming up soon, the error bars on these estimated division sales are getting fuzzier and fuzzier. And this chart also looks very much like Nvidia’s old divisional divide before and after the GenAI boom.

The thing to note is that the datacenter business has grown a factor of 8.1X since Q2 F2021, while those legacy chip businesses have grown by 1.3X over the same time. Imagine if Marvell had not bought IBM’s custom chip business out of GlobalFoundries as well as Inphi and Celestica AI. . . . Selling of the automotive chip business to Infineon was smart, too. It’s all hands on the GenAI deck. And it will not be surprising if Marvell sells off other divisions to get cash for maneuvering room and to have better focus.

What we really need to do is drill down into that datacenter business, and it would of course be helpful if Marvell would break this much larger business down into divisions. We have gotten enough hints and a few data points here and there from the Marvell top brass to build a model of how such divisions might be created and how much money they are driving. The US Securities and Exchange Commission should have rules about when a business that is clearly comprised of divisions needs to be financially reported as such. The loose rule at the SEC is that the way you run the business and talk about it internally is supposed to be the way you talk about it – in a very general sense, of course – to investors.

Here is my attempt to drill down into Marvell’s overall datacenter and AI-related datacenter products businesses and breaking that down into two main groups And here is a chart breaking out AI electro-optics from AI custom chips and then other datacenter products. (This does not include enterprise networking.) Anyway, take a gander:

As the GenAI boom was just getting started back in early 2023 – call it Marvell’s Q1 F2024 – the company had an AI business that was around $77 million, with on the order of $12 million in early custom ASICs through a deal with Amazon Web Services for Graviton chips and maybe $66 million in electro-optics component sales.

Fast forward to Q2 F2027, a little more than three years later, and I estimate that AI revenue for Marvell was $1.82 billion, up 90.9 percent year on year and 23.6X higher than three years ago. AI XPU sales slumped a little sequentially in the current quarter, to around $425 million, but that was up 43.1 percent and faster than the 20 percent or so growth that Marvell told Wall Street to expect a few quarters ago.

Electro-optical components continue to dominate the AI story at Marvell, with revenues of around $1.4 billion, up 97.2 percent, in my model. Other datacenter products sold outside of the AI customer set accounted for around $347 million, therefore, down 28.4 percent.

Add it all up, and Marvell had $2.74 billion in revenues, up 36.5 percent, with an operating income of $460 million, up 58.5 percent, and net income of $308 million, up 58.1 percent. The company has $3.93 billion in the bank, which it will need to fulfill its obligations to chip shepherding customers.

Looking ahead, Marvell is raising its guidance once again, and now says to expect around $3.15 billion in sales in Q3 F2027, which would be an increase of 51.8 percent year on year and up 15 percent sequentially. Matt Murphy, Marvell’s chairman and chief executive officer, said that growth will accelerate in Q4 2027. Notably, the first revenues from Google’s recently announced expanded partnership with Marvell hit in Q3 F2027.  The datacenter business is expected to grow by around 20 percent sequentially and by around 75 percent year on year in the third fiscal quarter.

Murphy sweetened the fiscal 2027 year’s revenues to $12 billion, up from $11.5 billion a quarter ago, and that puts Q4 F2027 at around $3.7 billion, up 66.4 percent year on year. The datacenter in general and AI specifically are driving this growth, obviously. If you do some math in pencil on a scrap piece of paper, custom CPUs and XPUs will represent about $2 billion in sales in F2027, rising at around 33 percent and well ahead of the 20 percent growth that Marvell was talking about a few quarters ago. That legacy comms and other chip business is expected to grow by a mere 10 percent or so in fiscal 2027.

As for fiscal 2028, Murphy upped the guidance by $1.5 billion from the prior quarter’s guidance to $18 billion, which is a 50 percent growth rate, and added that the datacenter business would grow by more than 60 percent in fiscal 2028. Scale up network components for UALink, ESUN, and NVSwitch networks as well as for the Celestial AI optical interposer are expected to be on the order of $300 million, with Celestial AI’s hardware representing about $150 million. The custom CPU and XPU accelerator business in F2028 is expected to more than double in fiscal 2028 and grow even faster in 2029, in part due to the Google deal but also because of chip projects that Marvell is shepherding for AWS and others.

item.title: VMware Intros Private AI Cloud, AI Factory As Workloads Shift To On-Prem
item.description:
Ongoing cost, sovereignty, and security issues that arise as enterprises move from experimentation with AI to large-scale production deployments are continuing to fuel the shift of AI workloads away from public cloud environments to on-premises private clouds and AI factories , which are becoming the dominant datacenter model for many organizations. Research firm Omdia is predicting global datacenter investments will climb to almost $1.6 trillion by 2030, and that this year, tech enterprises will spend more than $600 billion in AI infrastructure.

It’s a significant jump from traditional datacenters to AI factories, which Omdia defines as infrastructure designed to produce intelligence, with token production at its center and “characterized by ultra-high capital intensity, strong geopolitical attributes, and complex engineering barriers.”

Nvidia coined the term AI factory, which is just supercomputers running GenAI inference that crank out tokens to make money directly or to help get it in some fashion. OEMs like Dell, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and others offer their own AI factories, with many based largely on Nvidia GPUs and other offerings.

At the VMware Explore 2026 event this week in Las Vegas, VMware and its owner, Broadcom , are more tightly embracing the shift to on-premises AI production environments, building on its VMware Cloud Foundation 9 (VCF 9), introduced two years ago , with the introduction of its VMware Private AI Cloud and – at its foundation – the VMware AI Factory model-as-a-service offering.

In VCF 9, VMware introduced a number of features to address such challenges as cost and management of AI workloads, including NVMe memory tiering that company executives say can reduce per-host costs by as much as 42 percent and VMware AI Assistant, an interface for resolving complex issues arising from such areas as CPUs, memory, and hypervisors.

The latest moves – which includes enhancements to Tanzu and more capabilities around the critical security issue in AI – will help VMware users to more easily move their AI workloads into their own environments, according to Prashanth Shenoy, vice president of marketing for Broadcom’s VMware Cloud Foundation Division.

“We've seen as organizations are moving from pilot deployments of AI applications and workloads to more production deployments of AI done at scale, they are facing major challenges around cost and security when it comes to data privacy, resiliency, availability of the infrastructure,” Shenoy told journalists during a pre-Explore media briefing. “That is causing a lot of organizations to repatriate workloads and run some of the production AI workloads back to an on-premises and private cloud environment.”

He pointed to the results in VMware’s June survey of 1,800 IT decision-makers, with 56 percent saying that their organizations are running or planning to run production inference in a private cloud. Sixty-two percent are concerned about costs and 51 percent said they’re repatriating AI workloads due to security concerns. The survey also found that use of public clouds for such workloads fell 15 percent year-over-year to 41 percent.

“They are preferring private cloud to run their production workloads – be it inferencing, fine-tuning, rack kind of AI use cases – in a private cloud on-premises because of the cost and security environment,” he said, adding that VMware Private AI Cloud “helps address the cost efficiency issues that we can bring to our customers, the security in the frontier AI model-driven security landscape, as well as customers moving to an agentic way of building their AI applications as well as workflows.”

VCF 9 already supports CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators from multiple vendors and server hardware from OEMs and ODMs. Now comes Private AI Cloud, with VMware AI Factory at its foundation. VMware AI Factory includes VCF AI ReadyNodes from such hardware makers as Dell Technologies , Cisco Systems , Lenovo, and Supermicro , among others. In addition, it leverages AMD technologies , including its Instinct MI350 Series GPUs and open ROCm, an open software platform for GPU accelerators, AI, and HPC on AMD hardware.

The AI factories have been tested by VMware and parent company Broadcom , Shenoy said.

“This is very critical because we have seen more and more customers wanting to run AI where their data lives, not the other way around,” he said. “They want to bring data to the model and not model to the data. But building this entire AI infrastructure from the metal to the module is a very manual process, where they have to stand up the infrastructure, put together the server with the right GPU size and form factor, bring the networking, the storage requirements, the Kubernetes for container workloads, the AI software stack, and different kind of models, be it SLMs [small language models], LLMs, open source, and open-weight models.”

Instead, VMware through the AI factories delivers an entire integrated package, all orchestrated via MetalSoft’s platform, which offers a unified operation of the underlying hardware and software.

VMware, through its VCF 9, also is expanding to more than 150 the open and commercial AI models that can run on AI Factory can run, adding support for Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 , Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 , Alibaba’s Qwen 3.7-Max, NEC’s cotomi, and GLM 5.2 from Z.ai.

VMware is introducing new AI services, including the ability to share AI models between tenants and lines of business via isolated nameplates, ensuring security and eliminating the need to deploy the same models, AI Gateway for ensuring unified model governance between cloud and on-premises environments, and secure AI sandboxes, virtualized container spaces for isolating agent code execution. Highly secure sandboxes are a focus in the agentic AI field after instances of OpenAI and Anthropic agents broke out of sandboxes to compromise third-party IT environments.

Other security controls include TrueSource by Broadcom for verifying open source AI, enhancements to vDefend to include zero-trust security for agentic AI workloads, and agentic threat defense via VMware’s Avi Load Balancer, another tool for ensuring that agents don’t access unauthorized tools, run zero-day attacks, or exfiltrate sensitive data without guardrails.

Similarly, VMware enhanced Tanzu, its agent platform for Private AI Cloud, with stronger security features that include hardened agent sandboxes with a “deny-by-default” containment model. It isolates credentials to prevent prompt injection attacks and network access that isn’t authorized by users. AI-ready data foundations processes both structured and unstructured data on-site to help improve agents’ accuracy, lower the cost of tokens, and reduce hallucinations.

A ready-to-go harness is aimed at giving developers pre-approved skills for agents, workflow buildpacks, human-in-the-loop controls, and integrated memory services. There also is marketplace where developers and agents can security connected to vetted AI models and tools, while an AI gateway is available for monitoring and logging all actions an agent takes for compliance and auditing purposes.

Shenoy said such features are critical “because all of these autonomous AI agents generate and execute code dynamically, and that creates security risk without proper governance as to, ‘What can these agents access from a tool, from a data, which agents can talk to which other agent.’ This framework will sandbox the agents within isolated secure containers and regulate which tools and agents they can communicate with.”

item.title: In The Long Run, Nvidia NVSwitch Is The InfiniBand Of Scale Up AI Networks
item.description:
Way back in the dawn of time, there were two rival future I/O schemes for PCs and servers, and as the Dot Com boom roared along, they buried the hatchet and made a compromise that resulted in the InfiniBand ports and switched fabric as the I/O bus for all of computing.

But alas, the Dot Com bust came along, and everybody who agreed on this standard kicked it into the ditch and focused on Ethernet for point to point interconnect (like our PCs and servers have linking to the Internet or in-house networks) and for what we now call scale out networking for aggregating compute across many machine. Given the very tough economy, the industry also opted for an updated PCI-X and then PCI-Express bus for peripherals.

InfiniBand as a high performance, low latency interconnect was pulled out of the ashes by Voltaire and Mellanox Technologies, with Mellanox supplying switch ASICs and NICs and Voltaire making switches aimed at HPC ModSim workloads. Mellanox bought Voltaire for $218 million in November 2010 to consolidate its InfiniBand switching position. InfiniCon systems, founded by a bunch of ex-Unisys techies, got into the game and after many permutations became QLogic, the only real rival to Mellanox in the InfiniBand space, which was acquired by Intel for $125 million in January 2012 . (That QLogic team was spun out of Intel to become Cornelis Networks in September 2020 .) TopSpin was an InfiniBand switch player, and was bought by Cisco Systems in 2005. Sun Microsystems, under the guidance of co-founder Andy Bechtosheim, adopted InfiniBand as the clustering technology in its “Constellation” HPC clusters and made its own InfiniBand ASICs and NICs. Oracle continued this for a whole after it bought Sun Microsystems in April 2009 for $5.6 billion , and Big Larry even bought InfiniBand switch maker Xsigo Systems to bolster its position and then decided that Ethernet was its scale up, scale out, and scale across networking platform.

With the Ultra Ethernet Consortium founded in July 2023 , the idea is to marry the low latency and high bandwidth of InfiniBand and some of its quality of service and adaptive routing capabilities to the higher scalability, multitenancy, and quality of service features of Ethernet to make a scale out network that can beat InfiniBand, hands down, and AI clusters that aim to support 1 million endpoints. Ethernet is also making its way into the scale up domain of Nvidia’s NVSwitch interconnects for lashing GPU memories into one coherent, shared memory space for 72 accelerators with a means of expanding the network to support 576 devices if you don’t mind the latency hops.

For the record, I love InfiniBand, and I love NVSwitch. InfiniBand was the undisputed low latency leader for two and a half decades, and still has an advantage today, which is why I think Nvidia has made $25.74 billion in the trailing twelve fiscal months ending in July. This is almost the same as the $25.67 billion that I think Nvidia sold for Ethernet and NVSwitch interconnects combined. But this is probably peak InfiniBand for large clusters, with so many hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders moving to standardize on impending Ultra Ethernet technologies and Ethernet ASIC vendors like Broadcom, Cisco Systems, and even Nvidia itself driving down the port hop latency and the end to end latency in their Ethernet fabrics.

More than a decade ago, I wrote that InfiniBand was too quick to be killed by Ethernet , and I expect for InfiniBand to be around for a long time from Nvidia, which is pretty much the only supplier these days aside from some custom HPC interconnects in China that are based on InfiniBand – licensed and sanctioned by the formerly independent Mellanox but perhaps enhanced enough to not be called InfiniBand anymore. But Ethernet can definitely corral InfiniBand into a relative niche, given its scale advantages and wide compatibility with campus, edge, and datacenter networks. And looking ahead, NVswitch for scale up and Spectrum-X Ethernet for scale out are going to dominate Nvidia’s own sales. This is a customer pull, not a vendor push. Enterprises, for sure, are going to want Ethernet, and so do the AI model builders – even Meta Platforms, which has given InfiniBand its time in the limelight on earlier AI clusters.

The old adage in the networking space is that Ethernet always wins. And it does. And that is because it steals every good idea from any fabric that can be broadly applied across enterprise networks as well as nichey stuff in HPC and now AI. And what is true of the scale out network linking systems together into clusters and people to these systems will be equally true of the scale up network that is being used to lash together GPUs and XPUs in AI clusters. We are already seeing very fast Ethernet being used as a transport for other memory sharing approaches.

This includes UALink, which fired the first salvo at NVLink and NVSwitch when it was founded back in May 2024 by AMD, Broadcom, Cisco Systems, Google, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Intel, Meta Platforms, and Microsoft; significantly, AMD is using Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Ultra Ethernet switches to run the UALink protocol for the scale up network inside of its “Helios” racks. UALink is just a memory atomic protocol for linking XPUs and GPUs and if you want CPUs and DPUs to share memory, nothing will stop you. So is the ESUN protocol espoused by Meta Platforms and Microsoft, who were joined by AMD, Arista Networks, Arm, Cisco, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Marvell, Nvidia, OpenAI, and Oracle. Broadcom is part of the ESUN/SUE-T effort (two different layers in an Ethernet scale up stack, with SUE-T handling load balancing and other higher level functions), has walked away from UALink, and as far as we know is not interested in the NVLink/NVSwitch combo. But that may change if its CPU and XPU customers in its chip shepherding business decide they want to endorse NVSwitch as their rackscale fabric and use Nvidia-style racks in their datacenters for both their GPUs and their XPUs.

It is hard to say how this will all shake out.
